content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper study an interesting problem that improves user engagement in sequential recommendations. Considering that current rules of taking a break are manually settled, this paper propose to learning a user dependent and stationary policy to decide when to take a break.
Lotka-Volterra dynamics is used to model two patterns of users, drive to consume and intrinsic interest. 

A learning algorithm based this dynamics is proposed and is validated on a semi-synthetic public data.

content.title: Response to Reviewer ggoW
content.comment:
**“This paper aims to learn a policy that is independent of time step, which might limit the performance.”**  

Thank you for this comment - your observation is correct, but the implications are more nuanced. As our work takes the first step towards learning breaking policies, we intentionally focus on simple decision rules. One justification for considering static policies is that within the space of continuous LV dynamics, a well-known result states that static policies are “approximately optimal”; this relies on the “turnpike” property of LV systems [1], which states that for a time horizon $T$, the optimal *non-stationary* policy is in effect static for the majority of the time period (in particular, it will vary only in the beginning of the period and towards its end). Since the optimal non-stationary policy is typically hard to compute, static policies serve as practical and tractable proxies. Outside the space of LV systems, we agree that in principle, non-stationary policies can be more expressive; however, it is entirely unclear how - and even if - they can be learned, since this reduces to a non-trivial optimal control problem.  

**“This paper assumes that the behavior follows the Lotka-Volterra dynamics. Do the authors justify the assumption in real datasets?”**  

Please see our general response above, in which we address this point in context.  

**“What is the detail of the evaluation metric? There is no engagement metric in MovieLens.”**

Our experiments measure engagement using simulated user behavior. These simulations are anchored in the original dataset (MovieLens, or in our new experiment - Goodreads): specifically, we first fit a behavioral model to the real dataset (which includes user ratings or reviews), and then use this model to generate simulated temporal responses to recommendations. Since recommending breaks is a policy learning problem, our experimental evaluation requires us to address counterfactual outcomes, i.e., measure or anticipate eventual long-term engagement under different possible breaking policies for the same initial conditions. Using simulation is an established means for doing this, and has become a standard in the community of policy learning for recommendation (for example, see extensive discussions in [2,3]).

---
References:

[1] Optimal control and turnpike properties of the Lotka Volterra model [[Ibanez & Zuazua 2013](http://www.bcamath.org/documentos_public/archivos/personal/conferencias/LotkaVolterra.pdf)]   
[2] Recsim: A configurable simulation platform for recommender systems [[Ie et. al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.04847)]  
[3] Recommendation System Simulations: A Discussion of Two Key Challenges [[Chaney 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.02475)]

content.strength_and_weaknesses:
#Strength
1. The paper studies recommendation systems as human-centric ecosystems, and take one step towards sustainable design. This provides a new perspective on viewing recommender systems.  
2. The paper proposes to model user behavior as a dynamical system of Lotka-Volterra (LV) Predator-Prey equations to optimize engagement with breaks, where the effect of break policies is modeled by control variables. Such design is ingenious and innovative.

#Weakness
1. The paper needs to further explain the rationality of introducing LV dynamic systems. Under this model, the paper proposes two latent variables and analyzes their dynamical properties. There should be some online experimental results (e.g. A/B test) to verify the existence of such hidden variables and the dynamical properties of latent variables. Modeling the time-dependent relations as in Equation (2) seems not very convincing to me.
2. The experiment description is not clear enough. 
3. The experimental results are not sufficient. It would be much better to conduct online evaluation or offline evaluation on more semi-synthetic datasets.
4. The overall paper also needs an additional round of writing revision.

content.title: Response to Reviewer VBoA
content.comment:
**The rationality of introducing LV dynamic systems**

 As we discuss in our general response above, the main rationale in introducing LV dynamics into recommendation is to capture bi-directional feedback dynamics, which permit (and require) active conservation. None of the previously proposed models in the literature on learning to recommend permit this.   
Our particular choice of latent variables is based on psychological constructs; the idea that these act as resources that deplete in response to exposure is grounded in the literature on cognitive resource theory. We view our model as a plausible mechanism that is simple enough to analyze yet rich enough to generate complex behavioral patterns.  

**Clarity of experiments section**

Thank you for this comment, we will revise and clarify the exposition to our experimental setting. Please note that Appendix B includes additional experimental details.  

**Additional online evaluation or offline evaluation on more semi-synthetic datasets**

 As per your request, we have added a new experiment using an additional dataset of book reviews (GoodReads). Results are encouraging, and exhibit similar trends to those reported in our first experiment on movie ratings (MovieLens). Please see Appendix C.1 for details.

**Grammatical errors**

Thank you for pointing out such details. The updated revision has been corrected for grammatical errors. Please notify us if you discover any additional errors.

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper the authors study how recommenders could provide a personalized approach to recommending breaks to users that would still maximize long-term engagements.  The authors do this by assuming a particular dynamic model of user interest (Lotka-Volterra) and demonstrating how a policy could be learned for recommending breaks to users in conjunction with a recommender system.  They test this on simulated user dynamics on top of Movielens ratings data to demonstrate that their learned policy is more effective than alternative approaches.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
S1. The question of how to better incorporate user well being into recommender design and how we can leverage long term models to do so is an interesting and important question to study.
S2. Under the assumed model given, the paper is thorough in exploring the learning problem and demonstrating the efficacy of their learning approach.

W1. The assumed model of user dynamic is highly novel - this is a strength in that it has not been used in the recommender literature before (as far as I know) but the paper does not actually explain or demonstrate why this particular model is a good one.  The experiments do show that it is flexible for learning even assuming a more complex user model, but alternative framings of the problem (e.g. from Kleinberg et al 2022) are not compared with and no empirical evidence is given that this fits or benefits real users at all.

W2. The paper does not consider a lot of recent work and important aspects of recommender systems related to the actual items being recommended.  There is a large body of literature on diversity, dynamics of user interests within and across topics, additional signals of user feedback and satisfaction, leveraging surveys, etc.  In addition to not well contextualizing this work, this  both under-leverages state-of-the-art approaches for understanding user well being and is a limitation of the assumed user model, e.g. where user interest is unidimensinoal rather than evolving across many dimensions.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: The paper is relatively easy to read and the main ideas are clearly described.

Quality: The paper makes some strong assumptions in their problem framing that are in my opinion not sufficiently supported, but under those assumptions the paper is thorough in studying how to incorporate them into the recommender design and evaluating their methods' effectiveness.

Novetly: The question being studied and the model deployed is novel and I think would be of interest to other researchers.

Reproducibility: While I don't believe code is provided, I expect the methods could be reproduced.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the paper is thorough in exploring a novel design space for recommender systems.  However, I believe significant additional research would be needed to demonstrate that their assumed dynamics model is reflective of real users and that their proposed approach does lead to higher long term user satisfaction.  As a result, I do not believe the paper is ready for publication at ICLR.

content.title: Response to Reviewer ZJ5Y (part 1/2)
content.comment:
Thank you for your detailed comments and for taking the time to review our paper thoroughly. Please find below our detailed response to your inquiries. Overall, our feeling was that our viewpoints regarding goals and contributions are somewhat misaligned, and here we wish to realign them. We hope our comments herein, together with our general response above, aid in addressing your concerns, in which case we hope that you would be willing to reconsider your evaluation.  

**“The paper does not consider a lot of recent work and important aspects of recommender systems related to the actual items being recommended.”**  

Thank you for this comment. Our problem formulation intentionally decouples the *recommendation policy* ($\psi$) from the *breaking policy* ($\pi$). This allows us to abstract away the specifics of the recommendation policy, and focus entirely on optimizing breaks - which is our stated goal. As such, nothing restricts the recommendation policy from utilizing additional structure or information, and our approach is applicable to any general $\psi$.   

In terms of breaking policies, we certainly agree that utilizing additional structure is likely to be beneficial. However, given that our work is the first (to our knowledge) to explore the task of optimizing breaks, we believe it is only natural to begin by exploring simple models that operate on basic feedback; we hope our results convey that even this results in a highly non-trivial learning problem. There is certainly merit in studying more elaborate breaking policies - but we believe the fundamentals of this problem should be established first.  

Nonetheless, and in response to your comment, **we have added an additional experiment** in which we extend our breaking policy to incorporate additional feedback, in the form of temporally-sparse user-provided ratings (see Appendix C.2). Results show that indeed this leads to improved outcomes, which improve with additional feedback. We hope this serves to show that there is further potential in utilizing structure for learning to break in future works.  

As for additional related work, *we will gladly add references to recent methodological advances in recommendation systems*. Please note, however, that the literature we *do* survey (e.g., in Sec. 1.1) is that to which we feel our paper pertains - namely the literature that studies the role of learning in the dynamics of recommendation systems. In this literature, contributions typically come in the form of theoretical results on simplified models, or simulated experiments in controlled environments - of which our paper contributes both.  

(End of part 1/2)

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper1128 by Reviewer ZJ5Y

content.title: Response to Reviewer ZJ5Y (part 2/2)
content.comment:
(Start of part 2/2)

**“Alternative framings of the problem (e.g. from Kleinberg et al 2022) are not compared with”**  

Please note that while our work and [[Kleinberg et. al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.11776)] share conceptual similarities (i.e., both model behavior as a balance between two conflicting forces) - they are in fact quite distinct, in a way that makes their model inapplicable to our setting. Specifically, they consider discrete time, and ask when users leave the system - which is assumed to always occur at a geometric rate (one interpretation is that their model is useful for describing within-session engagement, rather than prolonged engagement).  

As for other explicit behavioral models - none of the works we are familiar with model how the *rate* of consumption varies (e.g., in continuous time) in response to recommendations: typically, works either model how preferences change over time, or whether users interact (or not) with content at predefined time-points. If there are however other framings that are suitable and that we have missed - we will gladly incorporate them within our work.  


**“The paper does not actually explain or demonstrate why this particular model is a good one”** 

Please see our detailed comments in the general response above.  


**“The paper makes some strong assumptions in their problem framing that are in my opinion not sufficiently supported”**  

As we note in our general response above, our work proposes the LV model as a *hypothesis class*, to be chosen at the discretion of the learner - and does not make any concrete assumptions on the nature of the true underlying data-generation process. In this sense, the LV model is not an “assumption”, but rather a possible modeling choice.  

Nonetheless, and in light of your comment, we have included an additional experiment in which we empirically evaluate our LV-based approach on data that is generated by a behavioral model that is entirely distinct (see Appendix C.3 for details). In particular, we set $\mathrm{TPP}$ to generate for each user interaction sequences that depend only on the quality of recommended items, and not on any latent internal states - this conforms to the behavioral model that is assumed (sometimes implicitly) in conventional recommendation methods (e.g., collaborative filtering). Our results here show that our approach learns a breaking policy that does not override the default policy when this is ineffectual.  


**“I believe significant additional research would be needed to demonstrate that their assumed dynamics model is reflective of real users, and that their proposed approach does lead to higher long term user satisfaction”**  

We agree with both claims - but at the same time, believe they rightfully lie outside of our paper’s scope. As we write in the general response above, our main contribution lies in establishing the learnability of a novel model class for breaking that is qualitatively different from current alternatives. True - our proposed model is not validated on real human users - but we do not see why this should be grounds for rejection. There is an extensive literature that studies recommendation - theoretically and in simulation - on simple and stylized models, and whose results often set the ground for practitioners and applied researchers to advance their findings towards the practical realm. We therefore kindly ask that our contributions be evaluated in this light.

content.title: General response to all reviewers (part 1/2)
content.comment:
We thank all reviewers for their careful reading and insightful comments. We were happy to learn that all reviewers were appreciative of the importance of the problem we study, and of the novelty of our proposed model. We begin by addressing the common points raised by several reviewers, and respond individually below.  
 
**1. Code**  
We would like to note that our original submission *does* include code, reproducing all experiments and plots. Please see the anonymized github link at the bottom of the introduction in Sec. 1 (also in the original submission), or visit https://github.com/lvml-iclr-2023/lvml.  

**2. New empirical results**  
Several new empirical results have been added according to the inquiries raised in the reviews:

* A replication of our results on an additional real dataset of book reviews (Goodreads) [in response to Rev. VBoA]
* An evaluation of a variation on our policy optimization approach, which can utilize additional user feedback (in particular, sparse item ratings) [in response to Rev. ZJ5Y]
* An experiment in which the data generation process (i.e., $\mathrm{TPP}$) follows a conventional, stateless user model, which is completely distinct from our LV model [in response to Rev. ZJ5Y]

Results in all three experiments are positive: the first experiment exhibits the same general trends as in the original; the second experiment shows that utilizing additional feedback improves the breaking policy and increases engagement; and the third experiment demonstrates how our approach is “safe”, in the sense that it does not recommend breaks needlessly. Details can be found in Appendix C, and our codebase has been updated to include these new results as well.  

**3. Contextualizing our work**  
In reading the reviews, we found two common concerns - namely that (i) our paper makes the assumption that user behavior is governed by LV dynamics, and relatedly, that (ii) LV dynamics may not necessarily be reflective of real user dynamics. Here we would like to address these by positioning our paper in a way which we hope calibrates expectations, and in ways which are more in line with the particular literature on dynamics in recommendations which we consider our paper as part of. We hope our comments herein help shed renewed light on our goals, and on what we view as our paper's main contributions.  

(End of part 1/2)

content.title: General response to all reviewers (part 2/2)
content.comment:
(Start of part 2/2)

**Learning under bi-directional feedback**

The basic premise of our work is that **real recommendation dynamics exhibit both positive *and* negative feedback**, which act as two opposing - but potentially balancing - forces. One benefit of this perspective is that it allows us to pose recommendation as a process which requires active conservation and long-term planning. Furthermore, it helps explain why suggested breaks, which have become common in practice, make sense as a strategy for promoting user well-being.   

To the best of our knowledge, all models of recommendation dynamics proposed so far in the literature consider at most one type of feedback (negative or positive). This is restrictive in two ways: First, uni-directional feedback implies that uncontrolled dynamics can either only explode or diminish - which is entirely unrealistic. Second, it makes it unclear whether it is at all possible to learn in the more realistic case of bi-directional feedback dynamics.  
 
In this context, we set out to explore how bi-directional feedback can be modeled, and whether it permits learnability. Since our work is the first to explore such dynamics, we propose and focus on simple dynamics - but which we nonetheless believe capture some of the essence of actual user behavior, and to some degree, are psychologically grounded (see ‘broader perspective’ in Sec. 1). Our goal in studying LV dynamics was to show that **learning is possible**, tractable, and even effective (to the extent that our experiments permit) under plausible bi-directional recommendation dynamics. Learnability is established by our theoretical results in Sec. 4.3, which we view as one of our main contributions (and which were not discussed in the reviews). Tractability is established by our proposed learning algorithm in Secs. 4.1, 4.2. Effectiveness is demonstrated by our semi-synthetic experiments in Sec. 5, and by our newly added experiments described above.  
 
**The LV model is a behavioral hypothesis class**

Some of the reviewers portrayed our work as "assuming" LV dynamics. Towards this, we would like to emphasize that none of our results *rely* on reality adhering to LV dynamics. Rather, and as we state, we propose LV dynamics as an *hypothesis class*, which we believe can be useful for predicting future user engagement in certain contexts. As such, LV dynamics are simply a modeling choice to be made by the learner.$^1$ Just as any other hypothesis class, performance under our proposed class relies on how well it fits the underlying data distribution; the benefit of our LV class is that it encodes bi-directional feedback - and in this it is unique. The tradeoff between expressivity and statistical efficiency is made precise in our error bound (Thm. 1); importantly, note that we allow the true underlying $\mathrm{TPP}$ to be entirely general, and make no assumptions on its relation to the LV model.  
 
**Experimental validation**

In principle, we certainly agree that effort should generally be made to validate the degree to which proposed theoretical models capture realistic behavior. However, to contextualize these concerns, please note that none of the other works in the literature we reference in Sec. 1.1 (and which we view our paper as part of) empirically validate their models - nor are they required to.$^2$ Providing real empirical evidence through experimentation is important, but presents entirely distinct challenges - some of which require experimental access to real recommendation systems - and which we view as orthogonal to our efforts. Given that our work: (i) studies a novel problem, (ii) proposes a novel, qualitatively-different model, (iii) establishes learnability theoretically, (iv) proposes a tractable learning algorithm, and (v) presents empirical results on semi-synthetic data - we believe that performing additional human experiments is important, but requires - and deserves - independent efforts beyond ours.  

Once again, we would like to thank the reviewers for their insightful and constructive remarks. 
Please do not hesitate to follow up during the second stage of discussion if you feel some questions remain unanswered.

---

Footnotes:
1. Similarly, collaborative filtering does not "assume" utility for users is linear (i.e., $y=\langle w,x \rangle$); it is simply a modeling choice, aimed at balancing functional expressivity with statistical efficiency and computational tractability. 
2. E.g., [[Krauth et. al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2011.07931.pdf)] who model "boredom", [[Leqi et. al. 2021](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2021/file/2109737282d2c2de4fc5534be26c9bb6-Paper.pdf)] who model "satiation", or [[Kalimeris et. al. 2021](https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1145/3447548.3467298)] who model preference shifts.
